metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) prediction specifically on trials where TTB and Tallying make strictly opposing predictions. Under the TTB theory, subjects will consistently choose the option favored by the first discriminating cue, yielding a high proportion. Under the Tallying theory, subjects will choose the option with more total feature wins, which is the exact opposite on these critical trials, yielding a very low proportion.

This metric isolates trials where Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) make opposite deterministic predictions. It computes the proportion of choices on these 'disagreement' trials that align with the Tallying heuristic. For data generated by Tallying, this proportion will be close to 1. For data generated by TTB, it will be close to 0. By restricting the calculation to trials with strict disagreement, it maximizes the quantitative contrast between the two theories and eliminates noise from agreement or guessing trials.

This metric isolates the critical trials where WADD and Tallying make diametrically opposite predictions. Specifically, when one option has the two most valid cues and the other has the three least valid cues, WADD chooses the former (since 0.95 + 0.85 > 0.6 + 0.55 + 0.5), while Tallying chooses the latter (since 3 features > 2 features). By computing the proportion of choices that align with WADD's prediction on these specific trials, we expect WADD to score significantly above 0.5 and Tallying to score significantly below 0.5, maximizing discrimination.

This metric isolates the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 2) where Tallying and WADD make completely opposite predictions. On these trials, one option wins on the three low-validity cues (favored by Tallying), while the other option wins on the two high-validity cues (favored by WADD). The metric computes the proportion of choices that are consistent with the Tallying heuristic. Tallying will yield a value significantly greater than 0.5, whereas WADD will yield a value significantly less than 0.5.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory's predicted choice. Since the experimental design systematically pits WADD against Take The Best (TTB) on 75% of the trials, this metric will be very high for WADD-simulated agents and very low for TTB-simulated agents, providing maximum discrimination with low variance.

This metric isolates the 'dissociation trials' where Take The Best (TTB) and Weighted Additive (WADD) theories make opposing predictions. It computes the proportion of choices on these trials that align with the TTB prediction. Under TTB, this value should be close to 1 (minus lapse rate and softmax noise), whereas under WADD, the value should be close to 0, providing a highly discriminative and stable contrast between the two models.

This metric calculates the proportion of times subjects choose the option favored by the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic (which has only the most valid cue, i.e., [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]) when it competes against an option strongly favored by the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy (which has 3 or 4 of the remaining cues). Under pure WADD, the compensatory value of the 3+ lower-validity cues easily overwhelms the single highest-validity cue, making choices for the TTB option extremely rare (limited to noise). In contrast, the Strategy Mixture theory predicts a substantially higher baseline probability for choosing the TTB option on these trials, driven by the fixed probabilistic weight placed on the TTB heuristic.

In the specific design used, trials 1, 3, 5, and 7 are constructed such that Option A possesses the most valid cue (cue 0), while Option B does not. However, Option B has a higher overall weighted sum (WADD score). Thus, a pure WADD model will consistently favor Option B, predicting a choice probability for A below 0.5. In contrast, the Strategy Mixture Theory assumes that a substantial portion of choices is driven by the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic, which unconditionally favors Option A on these trials. Measuring the proportion of Option A choices on this specific subset of trials will yield a significantly higher value under the Strategy Mixture Theory than under the pure WADD Theory.
